entries.meaning: To become four times as large, or to make something four times as large. ---
examples: Prices could quadruple if the harvest fails.
The city quadrupled its bus fleet in a decade.
Enrollment has quadrupled since 2010.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the city quadrupled its bus fleet), intransitive (prices quadrupled)

entries.meaning: To measure something and express it as a number. ---
examples: It is hard to quantify the damage to the brand.
Researchers quantified the effect at about nine percent.
The benefits have never been properly quantified.
entries.русский: измерять, определять количественно; оценивать в цифрах
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie in quantifies and quantified, but stays in quantifying.

entries.meaning: To cut something into four pieces. ---
examples: Quarter the apples and cut out the cores.
He quartered the pizza with a wheel cutter.
The chicken is sold whole or quartered.
entries.русский: делить на четыре части, разрезать на четвертинки

entries.meaning: To line up, or to put items in a line so they are handled one after another. ---
examples: Downloads queue automatically when the network is slow.
I queued three episodes for the flight.
Shoppers were queuing outside before dawn.
entries.русский: ставить в очередь, выстраиваться в очередь
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (I queued three episodes), intransitive (shoppers queued outside)
entries.contrast: Five letters, one sound: KYOO. The -ing form is written queuing or queueing; both are accepted.

entries.meaning: To become faster, or to make something faster. ---
examples: His steps quicken whenever he passes that dog.
She quickened her pace to catch the bus.
Interest in the case is quickening again.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she quickened her pace), intransitive (his pulse quickened)

entries.meaning: To say something clever and funny, usually in reply. ---
examples: He can quip his way out of any interview.
She quipped that the meeting could have been an email.
A reporter quipping about the delay got the biggest laugh.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he quipped that it could have been an email), intransitive (she quipped back)
entries.contrast: Short vowel, so the p doubles: quipped, quipping.

entries.meaning: To shake with small, rapid movements. ---
examples: Her hands quiver when she is nervous.
The arrow quivered in the target.
His voice was quivering by the end of the speech.

entries.meaning: To cause someone sharp physical or mental pain. ---
examples: Doubts rack him every time he has to decide.
A coughing fit racked her whole body.
He has been racking his brain for the name all morning.
entries.contrast: In rack your brain the spelling is rack, not wrack.

entries.meaning: To make someone adopt extreme political or religious views, or to become that way. ---
examples: Recruiters try to radicalize teenagers online.
The crackdown radicalized a whole generation.
He was radicalized during his first year abroad.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the crackdown radicalized a generation), intransitive (the movement radicalized quickly)

entries.meaning: To send a message by radio. ---
examples: Pilots radio the tower before landing.
The captain radioed for help at midnight.
They were radioing their position every hour.
entries.русский: передавать по радио, радировать; связаться по рации
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (radio the base), intransitive (he radioed for help)
entries.contrast: No -y change and no extra e: radios, radioed, radioing.

entries.meaning: To continue with great force, or to show violent anger. ---
examples: Wildfires rage through the canyon every fall.
The debate raged for three hours.
A storm has been raging off the coast since Tuesday.

entries.meaning: To complain about something angrily and at length. ---
examples: Columnists rail against the tax every spring.
He railed at the referee for ten minutes.
She has been railing against the decision all week.
entries.contrast: Takes against or at: rail against the rules, never rail the rules.

entries.meaning: To force something through, or force someone into a decision, without proper discussion. ---
examples: Do not let them railroad you into signing anything.
The committee railroaded the proposal through in one night.
Many believe he was railroaded by a rushed trial.

entries.meaning: To hit or push something with great force. ---
examples: Tugboats ram the ice to keep the channel open.
A truck rammed the barrier at the gate.
The post had been rammed two feet into the ground.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (a truck rammed the barrier), intransitive (the boat rammed into the dock)
entries.contrast: Short vowel, so the m doubles: rammed, ramming.

entries.meaning: To talk or write at length without a clear point. ---
examples: I ramble when I am nervous.
He rambled for twenty minutes about parking.
She kept rambling until someone changed the subject.

entries.meaning: To rush about violently, causing damage. ---
examples: Elephants sometimes rampage through the fields at night.
Fans rampaged through the streets after the loss.
A bear was rampaging through the campground.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed ram-PAYJ; the noun a rampage is stressed RAM-payj.

entries.meaning: To put things in a random order, or assign them by chance. ---
examples: The app can randomize the play order.
Researchers randomized patients into two groups.
The questions are randomized for every student.

entries.meaning: To keep causing annoyance or resentment long after the event. ---
examples: Small slights rankle for years.
The comment rankled him all evening.
The pay gap is still rankling with staff.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the comment rankled him), intransitive (the decision still rankles)

entries.meaning: To search a place roughly, leaving it in disorder, usually in order to steal. ---
examples: Thieves ransack empty houses during vacation season.
Someone ransacked the office over the weekend.
Every drawer had been ransacked.

entries.meaning: To speak or write angrily and at length. ---
examples: He will rant about the parking for an hour.
She ranted at the customer service desk.
Someone was ranting outside the courthouse.
entries.contrast: Usually with about or at: rant about the fees, rant at the staff.

entries.meaning: To invent reasonable-sounding explanations for behavior that is not reasonable. ---
examples: People rationalize almost any purchase.
He rationalized the lie as protecting his family.
She has rationalized every missed deadline this year.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he rationalized the lie), intransitive (we all rationalize)
entries.contrast: American spelling is rationalize; British writing uses rationalise.

entries.meaning: To talk about something with great enthusiasm. ---
examples: Critics rave about her second novel.
He raved about the tacos the whole drive home.
Everyone is raving about the new season.
entries.contrast: Takes about or over: rave about the food.

entries.meaning: To act or feel in response to something that has happened. ---
examples: Markets react badly to uncertainty.
She reacted calmly to the news.
The crowd was reacting to something we could not see.
entries.contrast: Takes to: react to the decision, never react the decision.

entries.meaning: To change something again, or to get used to a situation again after a change. ---
examples: Give your eyes a minute to readjust to the dark.
He readjusted the mirror before pulling out.
The family is still readjusting after the move.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he readjusted the mirror), intransitive (your eyes readjust slowly)

entries.meaning: To prepare someone or something for what is coming. ---
examples: Crews ready the plows before the first storm.
She readied herself for bad news.
The team is readying a response for the morning.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie in readies and readied, but stays in readying.

entries.meaning: To state again that something is still true or still your position. ---
examples: Both sides reaffirm the ceasefire every year.
The court reaffirmed its earlier ruling.
Support for the program has been reaffirmed in writing.

entries.meaning: To put something into a new position or arrangement. ---
examples: The shop can realign the front wheels in an hour.
The merger realigned the whole industry.
Districts are being realigned after the census.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the shop realigned the wheels), intransitive (the parties realigned after the vote)
entries.contrast: The g is silent: ree-uh-LYN.

entries.meaning: To give money, staff, or space to a different purpose than before. ---
examples: We can reallocate the unused budget.
The school reallocated two classrooms to the art program.
Funds have been reallocated to emergency housing.

entries.meaning: To be seen again after being absent. ---
examples: The symptoms usually reappear in cold weather.
He reappeared an hour later with coffee for everyone.
The file has reappeared in the trash folder.

entries.meaning: To put something back together, or for a group to gather again. ---
examples: Label the parts so you can reassemble the shelf.
The class reassembled on the field after the fire drill.
The engine was reassembled in a single day.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he reassembled the engine), intransitive (the class reassembled outside)

entries.meaning: To give someone a different job or post, or to give a task to someone else. ---
examples: Managers can reassign cases at any point.
The officer was reassigned to desk duty.
They are reassigning half the team to the new project.
entries.contrast: The g is silent: ree-uh-SYN.

entries.meaning: To arrange a new booking after the first one is canceled or changed. ---
examples: The agent can rebook you on the morning flight.
We rebooked the room for October.
Thousands of passengers are still being rebooked.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (we rebooked the room), intransitive (passengers had to rebook online)

entries.meaning: To give a company or product a new name and image. ---
examples: Struggling chains often rebrand rather than close.
The airline rebranded after the merger.
The store has been rebranded twice in five years.
entries.русский: проводить ребрендинг, менять название и образ
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they rebranded the chain), intransitive (the airline rebranded last year)

entries.meaning: To reject an offer or approach in a blunt, unfriendly way. ---
examples: Regulators regularly rebuff requests like this one.
She rebuffed every attempt to settle.
His offer was rebuffed within the hour.

entries.meaning: To argue with evidence that a claim or accusation is wrong. ---
examples: The defense will rebut each charge in turn.
She rebutted the figures with data of her own.
The central claim has never been rebutted.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the t doubles: rebutted, rebutting.

entries.meaning: To adjust an instrument, a plan, or a set of expectations to a new standard. ---
examples: Technicians recalibrate the sensors every six months.
After the first loss the coach recalibrated his goals for the season.
The scale has been recalibrated and finally reads correctly.

entries.meaning: To publicly take back something you said or believed before. ---
examples: Witnesses sometimes recant when they are threatened.
He recanted his confession a year after the trial.
She has never recanted a single word of her testimony.
entries.русский: отрекаться, отречься (от своих слов); отказываться от сказанного
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he recanted his confession), intransitive (the witness recanted on the stand)

entries.meaning: To go back over the main points of something briefly. ---
examples: Let me recapitulate the argument before we vote.
The last chapter recapitulated everything the author had claimed.
Having recapitulated the evidence, the lawyer sat down.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (recapitulate the argument), intransitive (let me recapitulate briefly)
entries.contrast: Recap is the everyday short form: she recapped the meeting.

entries.meaning: To take something back that was lost, or to bring back a feeling from the past. ---
examples: No photograph can recapture what that morning felt like.
Government troops recaptured the airport before dawn.
The band is recapturing the sound of their first album.

entries.meaning: To move something into a different official category. ---
examples: The agency may reclassify the drug next year.
Astronomers reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet.
Thousands of pages have been reclassified as secret.
entries.contrast: The -y turns into -ie-: reclassifies, reclassified.

entries.meaning: To lean back into a resting position, or to tip a seat backward. ---
examples: You may recline your seat once we are in the air.
She reclined on the porch swing with a cold drink.
He was reclining in the dentist's chair when the power went out.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (recline your seat), intransitive (he reclined on the sofa)

entries.meaning: To jerk back suddenly in fear or disgust. ---
examples: Most people recoil at the sight of blood.
She recoiled when he raised his hand.
The rifle kicked hard, recoiling into his shoulder.
entries.contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, REE-koyl; the verb on the second, rih-KOYL.

entries.meaning: To bring something back to mind after an effort. ---
examples: Two witnesses may recollect the same evening quite differently.
She recollected the exact words of the argument.
Having recollected the address, he wrote it on his hand.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (I can't recollect his name), intransitive (as far as I recollect)
entries.contrast: Recollect (rek-uh-LEKT) means remember; re-collect (ree-kuh-LEKT) means gather again.

entries.meaning: To begin again after a break. ---
examples: Negotiations will recommence on Monday morning.
Construction recommenced as soon as the permits came through.
Classes are recommencing next week after the holiday.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they recommenced work), intransitive (the talks recommenced)

entries.meaning: To promise again, with fresh seriousness, to do or support something. ---
examples: Both governments must recommit to the ceasefire.
After the scandal the company recommitted itself to safety.
He has recommitted to finishing his degree at night.
entries.русский: вновь посвящать себя, заново обязаться; вновь направлять (на рассмотрение)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she recommitted herself to the work), intransitive (both sides recommitted to the deal)
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the t doubles: recommitted, recommitting.

entries.meaning: To pay someone back for trouble, loss, or work done. ---
examples: The airline promised to recompense passengers for the delay.
The state recompensed the families of the victims.
Volunteers are rarely recompensed for their time.

entries.meaning: To make two people friendly again, or to make two facts or figures agree. ---
examples: It is hard to reconcile those two statements.
The bookkeeper reconciled the bank statement with the ledger.
They separated in March and have since reconciled.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reconcile the two accounts), intransitive (the couple reconciled)

entries.meaning: To repair and clean up used equipment so that it works like new. ---
examples: The shop can recondition the engine for half the price of a new one.
He reconditioned an old bike and sold it online.
The laptop is reconditioned, but it still has a warranty.

entries.meaning: To arrange the parts or settings of something in a new way. ---
examples: You can reconfigure the settings at any time.
They reconfigured the office into an open plan.
The network is being reconfigured over the weekend.

entries.meaning: To confirm something a second time so that it is certain. ---
examples: Please reconfirm your flight 24 hours before departure.
The office reconfirmed the appointment by email.
Everything has been reconfirmed with the hotel.

entries.meaning: To put something back together in its original form, or to add water to a dried food. ---
examples: Add warm water to reconstitute the dried mushrooms.
She reconstituted the powdered milk for the baby.
The commission was reconstituted with five new members.

entries.meaning: To get back money or time that you have lost or spent. ---
examples: The studio hopes to recoup its costs overseas.
He never recouped the money he lost on that deal.
The firm has recouped most of its investment already.

entries.meaning: To make something again so that it looks or feels exactly as it did before. ---
examples: The museum tried to recreate a 1920s kitchen.
Investigators recreated the crash second by second.
The set was recreated from three old photographs.
entries.contrast: Stress the last syllable: ree-kree-AYT 'make again'. The leisure noun recreation (rek-ree-AY-shuhn) is a different, unrelated word.

entries.meaning: To put right something that is wrong. ---
examples: We will rectify the error on your next bill.
The mechanic rectified the fault in ten minutes.
Nothing has been rectified since my last complaint.
entries.contrast: The -y turns into -ie-: rectifies, rectified.

entries.meaning: To become red, or to make something red. ---
examples: Her cheeks redden whenever anyone mentions his name.
The maple leaves reddened early that fall.
He stood there reddening while the whole class laughed.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (his face reddened), transitive (the sunset reddened the water)

entries.meaning: To give a room or building new paint, paper, or furnishings. ---
examples: We plan to redecorate the living room this spring.
They redecorated the whole apartment in one weekend.
The hotel is redecorating its top two floors.
entries.русский: переделывать интерьер, заново отделывать; делать ремонт
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (redecorate the kitchen), intransitive (we redecorate every few years)

entries.meaning: To change the meaning or limits of something. ---
examples: The ruling could redefine what counts as free speech.
The internet redefined how we read the news.
Marriage has been redefined by law in many countries.

entries.meaning: To move people, troops, or resources to a different place or task. ---
examples: The company will redeploy staff to the new warehouse.
Troops were redeployed to the northern border.
They are redeploying money from marketing into research.

entries.meaning: To design something again in a different way. ---
examples: They want to redesign the whole website.
Engineers redesigned the brake system after the recall.
The packaging has been completely redesigned.
entries.contrast: The noun is usually stressed first, REE-dih-zyn; the verb on the last syllable, ree-dih-ZYN.

entries.meaning: To rebuild an area or property so that it can be used in a new way. ---
examples: The city plans to redevelop the old rail yard.
A local firm redeveloped the factory into apartments.
That whole block is being redeveloped as affordable housing.

entries.meaning: To call the same phone number again. ---
examples: If the line is busy, just redial.
He redialed the number six times before anyone picked up.
She kept redialing until the office finally opened.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (redial the number), intransitive (if it's busy, just redial)
entries.contrast: American English keeps one l: redialed, redialing. British English doubles it: redialled.

entries.meaning: To send someone or something a different way. ---
examples: Police had to redirect traffic around the parade.
The old link redirected me to a page that no longer exists.
Funds are being redirected to emergency housing.

entries.meaning: To find or enjoy again something that had been forgotten. ---
examples: Many adults rediscover hobbies they loved as children.
Scholars rediscovered the manuscript in a church attic.
He is rediscovering how much he likes to cook.
entries.русский: вновь открывать для себя, заново обретать

entries.meaning: To share something out again, in different proportions. ---
examples: The plan would redistribute wealth through higher taxes.
Aid workers redistributed the supplies among four camps.
Seats in the House are redistributed after every census.

entries.meaning: To redraw the boundaries of voting or school districts. ---
examples: States redistrict after every census.
The legislature redistricted strictly along party lines.
The county is redistricting its school zones this summer.
entries.русский: перекраивать избирательные округа, изменять границы округов
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they redistricted the county), intransitive (states redistrict every ten years)

entries.meaning: To refuse loans, insurance, or services to people because of the neighborhood they live in. ---
examples: Banks used to redline entire neighborhoods.
Insurers redlined the area for nearly forty years.
Those blocks were redlined long before anyone living there was born.
entries.русский: отказывать в услугах жителям района (дискриминация); помечать красным
entries.contrast: In offices redline also means to mark up a draft with changes: the lawyer redlined the contract.

entries.meaning: To greatly increase an effort that is already under way. ---
examples: We must redouble our efforts before the deadline.
The search party redoubled its efforts after dark.
Critics have redoubled their attacks on the bill.

entries.meaning: To put right a wrong or an unfair situation. ---
examples: The law is meant to redress decades of unequal pay.
The settlement redressed only part of the harm.
Old wrongs are slowly being redressed.
entries.contrast: The noun meaning 'compensation' is often REE-dres; the verb is rih-DRES.

entries.meaning: To stagger, or to be badly shaken by a shock. ---
examples: Whole towns still reel from the flooding.
He reeled backward when the door swung open.
The market is reeling after another rate hike.

entries.meaning: To elect someone again to the same office. ---
examples: Voters may reelect the mayor for a third term.
She was reelected by a wide margin.
The party is spending millions on reelecting its senators.
entries.contrast: Often written with a hyphen, re-elect, to keep the two e's apart.

entries.meaning: To appear again after being absent or hidden. ---
examples: Old rivalries tend to reemerge during elections.
The singer reemerged after ten years of silence.
A worrying pattern is reemerging in the data.
entries.contrast: Often hyphenated in print: re-emerge.

entries.meaning: To go into a place or situation again, or to type something in again. ---
examples: The capsule will reenter the atmosphere at dawn.
She reentered the workforce after raising three children.
The password has to be reentered every single time.
entries.русский: вновь входить, вновь вступать; повторно вводить
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reenter the building), intransitive (the capsule reentered safely)
entries.contrast: Often hyphenated in print: re-enter.

entries.meaning: To set something up again after it has been broken off or lost. ---
examples: The two countries hope to reestablish trade ties.
Engineers reestablished contact with the satellite on Tuesday.
Order was quickly reestablished in the courtroom.

entries.meaning: To think again about the value or wisdom of something. ---
examples: You should reevaluate the plan before spending more.
The doctor reevaluated her treatment after the scan.
We are reevaluating every supplier this quarter.

entries.meaning: To rewrite computer code so that it is cleaner without changing what it does. ---
examples: We should refactor this function before adding anything else.
She refactored the login code in a single afternoon.
The module has been refactored twice this month.
entries.русский: рефакторить, переписывать код, не меняя поведения

entries.meaning: To direct attention or a lens onto something different. ---
examples: Let's refocus on the main question.
The campaign refocused on health care after the debate.
He is refocusing his energy on his family.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (refocus the camera), intransitive (let's refocus)
entries.contrast: American English keeps one s: refocused, refocusing.

entries.meaning: To change the layout or format of a document, disk, or program. ---
examples: You will have to reformat the drive before installing it.
He reformatted the whole report to fit on two pages.
The show is being reformatted for streaming.
entries.contrast: The final t doubles: reformatted, reformatting.

entries.meaning: To express something in a new way, or to change the ingredients of a product. ---
examples: Try to reformulate the question more simply.
The company reformulated the drink without sugar.
The policy has been reformulated three times this year.

entries.meaning: To present a problem or idea from a different point of view. ---
examples: A good therapist helps you reframe the problem.
She reframed the failure as a useful experiment.
The debate is being reframed as a question of cost.
entries.русский: переосмысливать, переосмыслить; представлять в ином свете

entries.meaning: To get back something you had lost. ---
examples: It takes months to regain that kind of strength.
He regained consciousness in the ambulance.
The team has regained first place in the division.
entries.русский: вновь обретать, вернуть себе; восстанавливать, восстановить

entries.meaning: To entertain someone generously with stories, food, or drink. ---
examples: He loves to regale guests with stories from the road.
She regaled us with tales of her winter in Alaska.
The children were regaled with cake and ice cream.
entries.contrast: Regale almost always takes with: regale someone with stories.

entries.meaning: To give away a present that someone gave to you. ---
examples: It is fine to regift something you will never use.
She regifted the candle set to her neighbor.
He has been regifting the same fruitcake for years.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she regifted the vase), intransitive (everybody regifts)

entries.meaning: To go back to an earlier and worse state. ---
examples: Patients sometimes regress under stress.
His reading regressed over the long summer.
The country is regressing toward older, harsher laws.
entries.русский: регрессировать, откатываться назад; возвращаться к прежнему состоянию
entries.contrast: The noun is REE-gres; the verb is rih-GRES.

entries.meaning: To bring swallowed food back up, or to repeat information without understanding it. ---
examples: Gulls regurgitate food for their chicks.
He simply regurgitated the textbook in his essay.
Students are tired of regurgitating facts they cannot explain.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (gulls regurgitate food), intransitive (the bird regurgitated)

entries.meaning: To bring an injured body part or a run-down building back into good condition. ---
examples: They buy old houses and rehab them for resale.
He rehabbed his shoulder for eight months.
She is rehabbing a knee injury and hopes to play in May.
entries.contrast: The final b doubles: rehabbed, rehabbing.

entries.meaning: To go over old material or old arguments again without adding anything new. ---
examples: I don't want to rehash that argument again.
The sequel simply rehashed the first movie.
They spent the whole evening rehashing old grievances.
entries.русский: пережёвывать одно и то же, повторять старое
entries.contrast: The noun is REE-hash; the verb is usually ree-HASH.

entries.meaning: To take back an employee you had let go. ---
examples: The plant promised to rehire the laid-off workers.
They rehired her at a higher salary.
Two of the fired managers have quietly been rehired.
entries.русский: снова нанимать, нанять повторно; восстанавливать на работе

entries.meaning: To start burning again, or to bring an argument or feeling back to life. ---
examples: The verdict could reignite the protests.
His comments reignited a debate that had gone quiet.
Old tensions are reigniting along the border.
entries.русский: вновь разжигать, вновь разжечь; вновь вспыхивать
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the verdict reignited the protests), intransitive (the fire reignited overnight)

entries.meaning: To think about something familiar in a completely new way. ---
examples: The director wanted to reimagine the story for today's audience.
They reimagined the old library as a community center.
The park has been reimagined as a wetland.

entries.meaning: To put a rule, tax, or restriction back into force. ---
examples: Officials may reimpose the mask requirement this winter.
Washington reimposed sanctions in January.
A curfew has been reimposed in three districts.

entries.meaning: To be born again in a new body, or to come back in a new form. ---
examples: Some traditions teach that souls reincarnate many times.
He joked that he had been reincarnated as a house cat.
The old theater is reincarnating as a bookstore and cafe.
entries.русский: перевоплощать, перевоплощаться; возрождать в новом облике
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reincarnated as a cat), intransitive (souls reincarnate)

entries.meaning: To infect someone or something a second time with the same disease. ---
examples: Touching the wound can reinfect it.
He reinfected half the office within a week.
Several patients were reinfected within a few months.

entries.meaning: To hurt again a part of the body that was hurt before. ---
examples: Come back too soon and you will reinjure the ankle.
He reinjured his hamstring in the second half.
She has reinjured the same knee twice this year.

entries.meaning: To bring someone or something back into a group or society. ---
examples: These programs help former inmates reintegrate into society.
The refugee children were reintegrated into local schools.
He is slowly reintegrating after two years abroad.
entries.русский: реинтегрировать, возвращать в общество; вновь объединять
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reintegrate the refugees), intransitive (he is reintegrating slowly)

entries.meaning: To explain or understand something in a new way. ---
examples: Each generation will reinterpret the constitution.
The court reinterpreted the statute very narrowly.
The play has been reinterpreted for a modern audience.

entries.meaning: To bring something back after it has been absent or discontinued. ---
examples: Lawmakers plan to reintroduce the bill in the fall.
Biologists reintroduced wolves to the park in 1995.
Solid foods are reintroduced one at a time.
entries.русский: вновь вводить, вновь ввести; вновь заселять (вид)

entries.meaning: To make something completely new again, especially yourself or your work. ---
examples: There is no need to reinvent the wheel.
She reinvented herself as a photographer at fifty.
The brand has reinvented itself three times in a decade.

entries.meaning: To put earnings back into a business or fund instead of spending them. ---
examples: Most owners reinvest their profits in the business.
He reinvested the dividends automatically.
The city is reinvesting in its public schools.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reinvest the profits), intransitive (we reinvest every year)

entries.meaning: To give fresh energy and strength to something that had grown tired. ---
examples: A new coach could reinvigorate the whole team.
The grant reinvigorated a department that had nearly closed.
Downtown has been reinvigorated by the new rail line.

entries.meaning: To publish or give out something again. ---
examples: The label plans to reissue the album on vinyl.
The state reissued his license after the hearing.
The novel is being reissued with a new introduction.

entries.meaning: To become a member of a group again, or to come back to people you had left. ---
examples: He hopes to rejoin the team next season.
She rejoined the company after two years away.
Members who quit are rejoining in large numbers.
entries.русский: вновь присоединяться, вновь вступать; возвращаться (в организацию)

entries.meaning: To make someone or something feel young, fresh, and lively again. ---
examples: A week at the lake can rejuvenate anyone.
The festival rejuvenated a downtown that had gone quiet.
She came back from vacation completely rejuvenated.

entries.meaning: To bring back a feeling, interest, or relationship that had faded. ---
examples: A trip home can rekindle old friendships.
The letter rekindled her interest in painting.
Their romance was rekindled at a class reunion.

entries.meaning: To make pain, worry, or pressure less severe, or to take over someone's duty. ---
examples: Two aspirin should relieve the headache.
A week of rain relieved the drought.
The night nurse is relieving her at eleven.
entries.русский: облегчать, облегчить; снимать (боль, напряжение); сменять (на посту)
entries.contrast: Spelled -ie-: relieve, relieved — compare the noun relief.

entries.meaning: To enjoy something greatly and openly. ---
examples: Some players relish the pressure of a big game.
He relished every minute of the argument.
She is not relishing the long drive back.

entries.meaning: To experience something from the past again, usually in memory or imagination. ---
examples: Veterans often relive the same night in their dreams.
She relived the crash every time she drove past that corner.
He has been reliving his college years all week.
entries.contrast: Not relieve /rɪˈliːv/ (ri-LEEV), which means to take pain or pressure away.

entries.meaning: To send a case back to a lower court, or to send a defendant back into custody. ---
examples: Appeals courts often remand cases for a new hearing.
The judge remanded him to county jail without bail.
The lawsuit was remanded to state court last month.
entries.русский: возвращать (дело) на новое рассмотрение; заключать под стражу

entries.meaning: To produce a new, better-quality version of a recording or film from the original source. ---
examples: The studio plans to remaster the whole trilogy in 4K.
They remastered the album from the original tapes.
A remastered version streams next week.

entries.meaning: To clean up contamination or fix a serious problem in a place or a program. ---
examples: The state will pay to remediate the contaminated soil.
The district remediated the lead problem over the summer.
Crews are remediating mold in three schools.

entries.meaning: To send money in payment to a person or office at a distance. ---
examples: Workers abroad remit billions of dollars to their families every year.
The company remitted the sales tax to the state.
Payment must be remitted within thirty days.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (remit the balance), intransitive (please remit by Friday)
entries.contrast: The t doubles before an ending: remit → remitted → remitting.

entries.meaning: To protest or argue forcefully with someone about something you think is wrong. ---
examples: Parents came to remonstrate with the principal about the new rules.
He remonstrated loudly, but the referee waved him away.
She stood at the counter remonstrating with the clerk for ten minutes.
entries.contrast: You remonstrate with a person about or over a thing.

entries.meaning: To pay someone for work they have done or costs they have carried. ---
examples: Good firms remunerate their staff fairly.
Panel members were remunerated for each day of hearings.
The lab is remunerating volunteers out of grant money.
entries.contrast: Note the order of the letters: re-MU-ne-rate, not "renumerate" — that spelling is simply wrong.

entries.meaning: To meet someone at an arranged place and time. ---
examples: The two boats rendezvous at dawn off the coast.
We rendezvoused with the guide at the trailhead.
The capsule is rendezvousing with the station tonight.
entries.contrast: The final s is silent: RAHN-day-voo, past RAHN-day-vood. Only the third-person rendezvouses has a spoken -z (RAHN-day-vooz).

entries.meaning: To break a promise or go back on an agreement. ---
examples: Politicians who renege on their promises lose voters fast.
The buyer reneged on the deal a week before closing.
They accused the city of reneging on the contract.
entries.contrast: Always renege on something. The final e drops before -ing: renege → reneging.

entries.meaning: To discuss an existing agreement again in order to change its terms. ---
examples: The team wants to renegotiate his contract before the season starts.
We renegotiated the loan at a lower rate.
The treaty is being renegotiated in Geneva.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (renegotiate the contract), intransitive (renegotiate with the lender)

entries.meaning: To order a supply of something again, or to arrange things in a different sequence. ---
examples: Call the supplier and reorder the filters.
She reordered the slides so the chart came first.
We have been reordering the same part every spring.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reorder the filters), intransitive (we reorder every month)

entries.meaning: To turn something, or yourself, in a new direction or toward a new purpose. ---
examples: The company plans to reorient itself toward electric vehicles.
After the layoffs he reoriented his career around teaching.
They are reorienting the whole program around online classes.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reorient the strategy), intransitive (reorient after a long flight)

entries.meaning: To put something in new packaging, or to present an old idea in a new form. ---
examples: Stores often repackage returned goods before selling them again.
The senator simply repackaged an old proposal with a new name.
The show is being repackaged for a younger audience.
entries.русский: переупаковывать, переупаковать; подавать в новом виде

entries.meaning: To send a person, money, or object back to the country it came from. ---
examples: The museum agreed to repatriate the looted artifacts.
Thousands of workers were repatriated after the border closed.
The company is repatriating profits held overseas.

entries.meaning: To feel deep regret for something you have done wrong. ---
examples: The preacher urged the crowd to repent.
He repented of the way he had treated his family.
She has never repented a single word of it.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (he repented of his lies), transitive (she repented her decision)
entries.contrast: In the intransitive use it takes of: repent of your mistakes.

entries.meaning: To move something into a different position, or to present a product or person in a new way. ---
examples: The nurse helped him reposition the pillow.
The brand repositioned itself as a budget option.
They are repositioning the satellite dish for a better signal.

entries.meaning: To take back goods from a buyer who has not kept up the payments. ---
examples: Lenders can repossess a car after three missed payments.
The bank repossessed their house last spring.
He worked two jobs to keep the truck from being repossessed.

entries.meaning: To move a plant into a different, usually larger, pot. ---
examples: Repot the seedlings once they have four leaves.
She repotted the fern in something bigger.
Most houseplants need to be repotted every couple of years.
entries.contrast: The t doubles before an ending: repot → repotted → repotting.

entries.meaning: To hold back a feeling or an impulse, or to put down opposition by force. ---
examples: He tried to repress a smile during the speech.
The regime repressed every attempt to protest.
Those memories had been repressed for years.

entries.meaning: To cancel or delay a punishment, or to save something from being shut down. ---
examples: Only the governor can reprieve a condemned prisoner.
The court reprieved him three hours before the execution.
The neighborhood library has been reprieved for another year.

entries.meaning: To perform or take on a role, song, or part again. ---
examples: She will reprise her role in the sequel.
The band reprised the chorus one last time.
He is reprising the part he played on Broadway.
entries.contrast: Say ri-PREEZ, not "ri-PRYZ". The noun reprisal (revenge) is a different word: /rɪˈpraɪzəl/.

entries.meaning: To give a machine, or a habit of mind, a new set of instructions. ---
examples: You can reprogram the thermostat from your phone.
The dealer reprogrammed the key fob in ten minutes.
Therapy is partly about reprogramming old reactions.
entries.contrast: The m doubles: reprogrammed, reprogramming — the single-m spellings are rare in American writing.

entries.meaning: To reject something publicly and completely, refusing to accept or be bound by it. ---
examples: Party leaders were quick to repudiate the remarks.
He repudiated the confession as soon as he had a lawyer.
The country has repudiated its foreign debt twice.

entries.meaning: To drive back an attack, or to fill someone with disgust. ---
examples: Fresh troops helped repulse the attack.
The smell of the kitchen repulsed her.
Voters were repulsed by the tone of the ads.
entries.contrast: Two senses: repulse an attack = push it back; be repulsed by something = be disgusted by it.

entries.meaning: To use something for a purpose other than the one it was made for. ---
examples: The city wants to repurpose the old mill as apartments.
She repurposed an old door as a desktop.
They are repurposing the footage for a documentary.

entries.meaning: To demand or order supplies through an official request, especially by an army or an agency. ---
examples: Units can requisition extra fuel through headquarters.
The army requisitioned every truck in the village.
New laptops have been requisitioned for the whole department.

entries.meaning: To send traffic, a flight, or a delivery along a different route. ---
examples: Crews had to reroute traffic around the sinkhole.
The storm rerouted dozens of flights to Denver.
Buses are being rerouted through downtown all week.
entries.contrast: Americans say either ree-ROOT or ree-ROWT; both are accepted.

entries.meaning: To rearrange people or things into a different order or set of jobs. ---
examples: The coach may reshuffle the lineup before the playoffs.
The governor reshuffled her cabinet after the election.
Management is reshuffling the whole department again.

entries.meaning: To live in a particular place, or, of a power or quality, to belong to someone. ---
examples: Roughly eight million people reside in the metro area.
She resided in Ohio for most of her adult life.
Students residing on campus must register their cars.
entries.contrast: Formal. In everyday speech Americans say live. Power resides in or with a body: authority resides with the board.

entries.meaning: To turn to something unpleasant or extreme because nothing else has worked. ---
examples: Don't resort to threats when a phone call would do.
The city resorted to rationing water in August.
He won the seat without ever resorting to negative ads.
entries.contrast: Always resort to. The noun resort (a vacation hotel) is spelled the same but is a separate sense.

entries.meaning: To fill a place with loud sound, or to echo off its walls. ---
examples: Cheers resound through the arena after every goal.
The gunshot resounded across the valley.
The hall was resounding with applause.
entries.contrast: The -ing form doubles as an adjective meaning 'emphatic': a resounding success.

entries.meaning: To happen as the effect of something, or to have something as an effect. ---
examples: Long hours often result in careless mistakes.
The fire resulted from a faulty space heater.
Two flights were canceled, resulting in long lines at the counter.
entries.contrast: Opposite directions: result in names the outcome (the crash resulted in delays); result from names the cause (the delays resulted from the crash).

entries.meaning: To appear again after a long absence, or to put a new surface on something. ---
examples: Old rumors resurface every election year.
The video resurfaced years after it was filmed.
Crews are resurfacing the parking lot this week.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the rumor resurfaced), transitive (resurface the road)

entries.meaning: To sell goods to the public, or, of an item, to be sold at a stated price. ---
examples: The sneakers retail for about ninety dollars.
The chain retailed its own brand of coffee for years.
They are retailing the same product under a new name.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they retail furniture), intransitive (it retails for $40)
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable: REE-tayl.

entries.meaning: To slow down the growth, progress, or spread of something. ---
examples: Shade retards the ripening of the fruit.
The coating retarded the spread of the flames.
Engineers added a layer of foam, retarding the heat for crucial minutes.
entries.contrast: Technical and formal only. Applied to a person, the related adjective is a serious insult in American English — in everyday speech say slow down or delay.

entries.meaning: To make the motions and sounds of vomiting, with or without bringing anything up. ---
examples: The smell alone made him retch.
She retched twice before the medicine took effect.
He knelt by the sink, retching and shaking.
entries.русский: тужиться при рвоте, давиться рвотными позывами
entries.contrast: A homophone of wretch (a pitiable person), and not the same as reach /riːtʃ/.

entries.meaning: To re-equip a factory for new production, or to rebuild a plan or program for a new purpose. ---
examples: The plant will retool to build electric motors.
They retooled the whole ad campaign after the launch flopped.
The company is retooling its factories in Ohio.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (retool the factory), intransitive (the plant retooled for masks)

entries.meaning: To answer back quickly and sharply, especially to a criticism. ---
examples: Don't retort every time someone criticizes your work.
"I never said that," he retorted.
The senator has retorted that the report is politically motivated.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he retorted that it was a lie), intransitive (she retorted sharply)

entries.meaning: To go back over a route or a sequence of events in order to find something or understand it. ---
examples: If you lose your keys, retrace your steps.
Detectives retraced the victim's last evening hour by hour.
We spent the morning retracing the route on the map.
entries.русский: возвращаться по своим следам; восстанавливать (ход событий)

entries.meaning: To cut spending or pull back from commitments in order to survive harder times. ---
examples: When sales fall, small firms retrench fast.
The university retrenched after donations dried up.
Washington has been retrenching from commitments abroad.
entries.русский: сокращать расходы, урезать; отступать (с прежних позиций)
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the firm retrenched), transitive (retrench spending)

entries.meaning: To try a case in court a second time, or to attempt an action again. ---
examples: Prosecutors may retry the case in the fall.
The state retried him after the first jury deadlocked.
The app keeps retrying the connection.
entries.contrast: The y changes to i: retry → retries → retried, but stays in retrying.

entries.meaning: To bring a divided country, group, or family back together. ---
examples: The agency's job is to reunify children with their parents.
Germany reunified in 1990.
Hundreds of families have been reunified since the ruling.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reunify families), intransitive (the country reunified)
entries.contrast: The y changes to i: reunify → reunifies → reunified, but stays in reunifying.

entries.meaning: To take great, open pleasure in something. ---
examples: Some coaches revel in the pressure of a big game.
She reveled in the attention for a week.
He spent the afternoon reveling in his win.
entries.contrast: Takes in. American spelling keeps one l — reveled, reveling; British writes revelled, revelling.

entries.meaning: To echo loudly through a space, or to have effects that spread far beyond the event. ---
examples: Low notes reverberate through the whole building.
The verdict reverberated across the industry.
The blast was still reverberating when the alarms started.

entries.meaning: To feel deep respect and admiration for someone or something. ---
examples: Many players still revere their old coach.
Critics revered her early films.
He is revered as the founder of modern jazz.

entries.meaning: To criticize someone with hatred and contempt. ---
examples: Columnists revile him one week and quote him the next.
Fans reviled the trade for years afterward.
The law was reviled by both parties.

entries.meaning: To change something so completely that it works in an entirely new way. ---
examples: Cheap sensors could revolutionize farming.
The smartphone revolutionized the way we take pictures.
New drugs are revolutionizing cancer treatment.
entries.contrast: American spelling uses -ize; British writes revolutionise.

entries.meaning: To put new electrical wiring in a building or device, or to change deeply fixed habits of thinking. ---
examples: An electrician will have to rewire the whole basement.
They rewired the house before moving in.
Meditation may be slowly rewiring how he reacts to stress.

entries.meaning: To tease someone in a friendly way. ---
examples: His friends still rib him about that haircut.
The crew ribbed the new guy all morning.
She was only ribbing you.
entries.contrast: Informal, and the b doubles: rib → ribbed → ribbing.

entries.meaning: To bounce off a hard surface and fly away at an angle. ---
examples: Bullets ricochet off the steel plates.
The puck ricocheted into the net off a defender's skate.
Rocks came ricocheting down the slope.
entries.contrast: The final t is silent: RIK-uh-shay, past RIK-uh-shayd.

entries.meaning: To fill something with holes, or with faults and problems. ---
examples: Rust had begun to riddle the old fenders.
Gunfire riddled the side of the building.
The report was riddled with errors.
entries.contrast: Usually in the passive with with: riddled with bullets, riddled with debt.

entries.meaning: To improvise freely on a musical phrase or an idea, playing with variations on it. ---
examples: Comedians often riff on the day's headlines.
The guitarist riffed for a full minute before the singing started.
They were riffing about office life and had the whole room laughing.

entries.meaning: To turn quickly through the pages or edges of something with your fingers. ---
examples: Let me riffle through the folder and see if the receipt is there.
He riffled the deck twice before dealing.
She stood at the desk, riffling the pages of the report.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (riffle the pages), intransitive (she riffled through the file)
entries.contrast: Not the same as rifle /ˈraɪfəl/, which means to search roughly through someone's things.

entries.meaning: To search hurriedly through a place or container, usually in order to steal something. ---
examples: Burglars rifle the bedroom drawers first, looking for cash.
Someone had rifled his backpack while he was swimming.
She was rifling through her purse for the car keys.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (someone rifled her desk), intransitive (he rifled through the mail)
entries.contrast: Spelled like the gun, and the vowel is /aɪ/: RY-fuhl, not RIF-uhl.

entries.meaning: To put something back upright, or to correct something that is wrong. ---
examples: It takes two people to right a canoe in deep water.
The crew righted the overturned truck within an hour.
The commission exists for righting old injustices.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (right the canoe), intransitive (the ship slowly righted)
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like write and rite. The set phrase is right a wrong.

entries.meaning: To make someone angry or annoyed. ---
examples: Nothing riles him like being interrupted.
Her remark about the budget riled the whole committee.
The coach was clearly riled by the referee's call.

entries.meaning: To put something valuable in danger, or to act in a way that may have a bad result. ---
examples: I would not risk my savings on a company that new.
He risked his life pulling the driver out of the car.
They are risking a huge fine by ignoring the deadline.
entries.contrast: Risk is followed by an -ing form, never an infinitive: risk losing the job, not risk to lose.

entries.meaning: To be as good as, or nearly as good as, someone or something else. ---
examples: Few American cities rival New York for nightlife.
Last summer's heat rivaled the record set in 1936.
Their collection is rivaled only by the one in Chicago.
entries.contrast: American English keeps one l: rivaled, rivaling; British English writes rivalled, rivalling.

entries.meaning: To hold someone's attention completely, or to fasten metal plates with rivets. ---
examples: A good opening scene rivets the audience.
The testimony riveted the courtroom for three hours.
Her eyes stayed riveted on the screen.
entries.contrast: The t does not double, because the stress is on the first syllable: riveted, not rivetted.

entries.meaning: To rise or move extremely fast. ---
examples: Prices rocket every time there is bad news about the harvest.
The song rocketed to number one in a week.
Rents have been rocketing since the plant opened.

entries.meaning: To stir something into violent, unsettled motion, or to churn in that way. ---
examples: Rumors of a merger can roil the stock market for days.
The scandal roiled the party just before the election.
Storm clouds were roiling over the lake.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the news roiled markets), intransitive (the water roiled below the falls)

entries.meaning: To court someone, or to try to win someone over with attention and charm. ---
examples: Startups spend months trying to romance big investors.
He romanced her with flowers and long letters.
The candidate has been romancing donors all spring.

entries.meaning: To describe or imagine something as better and more beautiful than it really was. ---
examples: Movies tend to romanticize small-town life.
He romanticized his army years until he ran into an old comrade.
We have been romanticizing the past for decades.
entries.contrast: American English spells it -ize; British English writes romanticise.

entries.meaning: To share a rented room or apartment with someone, especially as a student. ---
examples: Two of my cousins room together in Boston.
I roomed with him for two years in college.
She is rooming with a friend until the lease starts.
entries.русский: снимать жильё вместе, жить с соседом
entries.contrast: The other person takes with: room with someone.

entries.meaning: To play in a rough, noisy, physical way. ---
examples: The puppies roughhouse until they fall asleep.
They roughhoused in the living room and knocked over a lamp.
Stop roughhousing near the stairs.
entries.contrast: The gh is silent and the vowel is /ʌ/, as in rough: RUF-howss.

entries.meaning: To stare at something, especially an accident, out of curiosity while driving or walking past. ---
examples: Drivers always rubberneck when they see flashing lights.
Traffic crawled because everyone rubbernecked at the crash.
The delay was caused by rubbernecking, not by the accident itself.

entries.meaning: To feel deep regret about something you did. ---
examples: You will rue the day you signed that contract.
He rued his decision to sell the house.
She has rued it ever since.
entries.contrast: The -ing form drops the e: ruing, not rueing. The common phrase is rue the day.

entries.meaning: To think about something slowly and at length. ---
examples: Give him a day to ruminate on the offer.
She ruminated over the letter all weekend.
He was still ruminating about the interview a month later.

entries.meaning: To search through a place or container by moving things around. ---
examples: I will rummage in the garage and see if the pump is there.
He rummaged through three boxes before he found the photo.
She was rummaging in her coat for change.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rummage the drawers), intransitive (rummage through a bag)

entries.meaning: To produce saliva, or to show eager desire for something. ---
examples: The smell of bacon makes me salivate.
Investors salivated over the first quarter's numbers.
The dogs start salivating as soon as they hear the can opener.

entries.meaning: To make something holy, or to give it an appearance of moral approval. ---
examples: Nothing can sanctify a policy that harms children.
The chapel was sanctified in 1890.
Custom has a way of sanctifying bad habits.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: sanctifies, sanctified, but sanctifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To pile sandbags against rising water, or to hide your real strength in order to trick an opponent. ---
examples: Volunteers sandbag the riverbank every spring.
The town sandbagged the levee before the storm hit.
He admitted he had been sandbagging so his handicap would stay high.
entries.русский: обкладывать мешками с песком; скрывать свои силы, водить за нос
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they sandbagged the levee), intransitive (he was sandbagging all night)
entries.contrast: The g doubles: sandbagged, sandbagging.

entries.meaning: To squeeze something tightly between two other things. ---
examples: They sandwich two lectures between the labs.
The bakery was sandwiched between a bank and a barbershop.
He spent the flight sandwiched in a middle seat.
entries.contrast: Almost always used with between: sandwiched between two buildings.

entries.meaning: To drain someone's strength, energy, or confidence little by little. ---
examples: Long meetings sap everyone's energy.
The heat sapped our strength within an hour.
Months of bad news had sapped her confidence.
entries.contrast: The p doubles: sapped, sapping.

entries.meaning: To walk in a showy, confident, gliding way. ---
examples: Models sashay down the runway in impossible shoes.
She sashayed into the meeting twenty minutes late.
He came sashaying through the door as if he owned the place.
entries.contrast: The -y follows a vowel, so nothing changes: sashayed, sashaying.

entries.meaning: To answer someone rudely, especially an adult or a person in authority. ---
examples: Do not sass your grandmother.
He sassed the referee and got thrown out of the game.
She was sassing the teacher all period.

entries.meaning: To satisfy a hunger or a desire completely, sometimes to excess. ---
examples: A bowl of soup will not satiate a hungry teenager.
The trip satiated her curiosity about the desert.
Protein is more satiating than sugar.
entries.contrast: The ti is pronounced /ʃ/: SAY-shee-ayt.

entries.meaning: To make fun of someone or something by imitating them in a mocking way. ---
examples: Late-night shows satirize whoever is in power.
The novel satirized Washington society.
He has been satirizing the tech industry for years.
entries.contrast: American satirize, British satirise. The noun satire is said SAT-eye-ur.

entries.meaning: To walk in a slow, relaxed, unhurried way. ---
examples: On Sundays they saunter through the park for hours.
He sauntered in an hour late with a coffee in his hand.
A cat came sauntering across the porch.

entries.meaning: To attack someone or something fiercely, either physically or in words. ---
examples: A pack of dogs can savage a calf in minutes.
The paper savaged the mayor's budget.
Her first novel was savaged by the critics.

entries.meaning: To burn someone or something with hot liquid or steam. ---
examples: Be careful not to scald yourself with the steam.
He scalded his hand on the kettle.
The coffee came out scalding hot.

entries.meaning: To resell tickets at a price far above the official one. ---
examples: People scalp playoff tickets right outside the stadium.
He scalped two seats for triple the face value.
Scalping is illegal in several states.

entries.meaning: To shock people by behaving in a way they consider immoral or improper. ---
examples: Very little seems to scandalize this generation.
Her divorce scandalized the small town.
He enjoys scandalizing his relatives at dinner.

entries.meaning: To blame someone unfairly for a problem that others caused. ---
examples: It is easy to scapegoat newcomers when the economy slows.
The company scapegoated a junior analyst for the loss.
He felt he was being scapegoated by his own team.
entries.русский: делать козлом отпущения, сваливать вину на

entries.meaning: To make secret plans, usually dishonest ones. ---
examples: The two of them scheme constantly to get out of chores.
He schemed for years to take over the family business.
They were scheming behind the director's back.
entries.contrast: The sch- here is /sk/: SKEEM, not SHEEM.

entries.meaning: To carry something heavy or to travel somewhere with effort — informal American English, from Yiddish. ---
examples: I do not want to schlep a suitcase through three airports.
We schlepped all the way to Brooklyn for dinner.
He spent the morning schlepping chairs in from the van.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (schlep the boxes upstairs), intransitive (we schlepped across town)
entries.contrast: The p doubles: schlepped, schlepping. Also spelled shlep.

entries.meaning: To train someone thoroughly in a skill or subject, and informally to defeat someone so completely that they learn a lesson. ---
examples: Good coaches school their players in the basics.
His father schooled him in carpentry from the age of ten.
The rookie got schooled by a thirty-eight-year-old veteran.

entries.meaning: To speak about something with scorn, treating it as ridiculous. ---
examples: Economists scoff at predictions like that.
He scoffed when I said I would finish by Friday.
She kept scoffing at the idea until it worked.
entries.contrast: What you mock takes at: scoff at an idea.

entries.meaning: To move or leave quickly, or to slide something a short distance. ---
examples: I have to scoot — my train leaves in ten minutes.
She scooted her chair closer to the fire.
The kids went scooting down the hall in their socks.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (scoot your chair closer), intransitive (I have to scoot)

entries.meaning: To make an angry face by drawing the eyebrows together. ---
examples: He scowls whenever the subject comes up.
The guard scowled at my passport photo.
She was scowling into her coffee all morning.

entries.meaning: To leave a place fast — informal, and often used as a sharp order. ---
examples: Tell those kids to scram.
He scrammed as soon as the porch light came on.
The cat scrams every time the vacuum comes out.
entries.contrast: The m doubles: scrammed, scramming.

entries.meaning: To write something quickly and untidily. ---
examples: Just scrawl your name at the bottom of the form.
Someone had scrawled a phone number on the napkin.
He was scrawling notes as fast as she talked.

entries.meaning: To spend as little money as possible, often by going without things. ---
examples: They scrimp all year to pay for one trip.
My grandparents scrimped and saved for a down payment.
We have been scrimping on groceries since the rent went up.
entries.contrast: You scrimp on a thing: scrimp on materials. The set phrase is scrimp and save.

entries.meaning: To get something by asking around or searching, rather than by paying for it. ---
examples: See if you can scrounge a couple of chairs from the other office.
He scrounged enough plywood to build a shed.
They were scrounging for firewood after dark.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (scrounge a ride), intransitive (scrounge for change)
entries.contrast: The silent e drops before -ing: scrounging.

entries.meaning: To squeeze or crush something into a smaller, wrinkled shape. ---
examples: Do not scrunch the receipt — I need it flat.
She scrunched the letter into a ball and threw it away.
The kids were scrunching their toes in the sand.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (scrunch the paper), intransitive (the gravel scrunched underfoot)

entries.meaning: To fight or struggle with someone briefly and in a disorderly way. ---
examples: Fans sometimes scuffle in the parking lot after a loss.
Protesters scuffled with police outside the courthouse.
Two players were scuffling near the bench.
entries.contrast: You scuffle with someone.

entries.meaning: To move quickly with short steps, the way a small animal does. ---
examples: Mice scurry along the baseboards at night.
Everyone scurried for cover when the rain started.
Waiters were scurrying between the tables.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: scurries, scurried, but scurrying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To formally withdraw from a country, union, or organization. ---
examples: A few counties have threatened to secede from the state.
South Carolina seceded in 1860.
Several regions are seriously talking about seceding.
entries.contrast: You secede from something. The noun is secession /sɪˈsɛʃən/.

entries.meaning: To keep someone, or yourself, away from other people. ---
examples: Writers often seclude themselves to finish a draft.
He secluded himself in a cabin for the whole winter.
The house sits on a secluded stretch of beach.

entries.meaning: To produce and release a substance, as a gland or a plant does. ---
examples: Sweat glands secrete a salty fluid.
The pancreas secreted too little insulin.
The tree protects itself by secreting a sticky resin.
entries.contrast: Stressed on the second syllable, suh-KREET, unlike the noun secret, SEE-krit.

entries.meaning: To divide something into separate parts or groups. ---
examples: Marketers segment customers by age and income.
The company segmented the report into four sections.
The market is now heavily segmented.

entries.meaning: To separate one group of people or things from another, especially by race. ---
examples: Some schools still segregate students by ability.
The city segregated its buses until the 1950s.
Waste has to be segregated before it can be recycled.

entries.meaning: To move smoothly from one subject, song, or scene to the next. ---
examples: Let me segue to the budget for a moment.
The interview segued into a discussion of his childhood.
She has a gift for segueing from small talk to business.
entries.contrast: Written segue but said SEG-way, and the -ing form keeps the e: segueing.

entries.meaning: To make a person or thing more aware of something, or more easily affected by it. ---
examples: Campaigns like this sensitize the public to the risks.
Years abroad had sensitized him to how strange his own customs looked.
Repeated exposure can leave the skin sensitized.
entries.contrast: The opposite is desensitize. British English writes sensitise.

entries.meaning: To state officially the punishment that a court gives a guilty person. ---
examples: A judge can sentence him to as much as ten years.
The court sentenced her to community service.
He is being sentenced next Tuesday.
entries.contrast: The punishment takes to: sentenced to five years. The same word is also the everyday noun for a group of words.

entries.meaning: To keep a person or thing apart from others, especially for legal or safety reasons. ---
examples: The judge may sequester the jury during deliberations.
The witnesses were sequestered in separate rooms.
Forests help by sequestering carbon.

entries.meaning: To publish or broadcast a story in separate installments. ---
examples: Magazines used to serialize novels chapter by chapter.
Dickens serialized most of his books.
The paper is serializing her memoir this month.

entries.meaning: To chain a person's wrists or ankles, or to restrict someone severely. ---
examples: Outdated rules shackle small businesses.
The prisoner was shackled to the bench.
New debt is shackling the next generation.

entries.meaning: To treat someone unfairly, especially by cheating them out of money or credit — informal. ---
examples: Landlords who shaft their tenants eventually get sued.
He felt the company had shafted him on the bonus.
Freelancers keep getting shafted by late payments.

entries.meaning: To put a blade into its cover, or to cover something in a protective layer. ---
examples: Soldiers sheathe their swords at the command.
He wiped the knife carefully before sheathing it.
The tower is sheathed in copper.
entries.contrast: The noun sheath /ʃiːθ/ ends in a voiceless th; the verb sheathe /ʃiːð/ ends in -the, with the voiced th of this.

entries.meaning: To fire heavy artillery at a place, or to take nuts, peas, or seeds out of their shells. ---
examples: Sit with me and shell these peas.
Artillery shelled the city for three nights.
The village has been shelled twice this month.
entries.contrast: Shell out is a separate phrasal verb and means to pay, usually unwillingly.

entries.meaning: To promote something enthusiastically while pretending to be an ordinary, unpaid supporter. ---
examples: Influencers shill for whatever brand pays the most.
He shilled for the casino at every event in town.
She was accused of shilling a coin she secretly owned.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (shill a product), intransitive (shill for a company)
entries.contrast: You shill for a company or a candidate.

entries.meaning: To move with quick shakes from side to side, or to wobble that way. ---
examples: The steering wheel starts to shimmy above sixty.
She shimmied through the gap in the fence.
He was shimmying up the drainpipe when the light came on.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: shimmies, shimmied, but shimmying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To avoid work or a responsibility that you ought to take on. ---
examples: Nobody on this crew shirks the dirty jobs.
He was fired for shirking his duties.
She has never shirked a hard assignment.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (shirk your duties), intransitive (he never shirks)

entries.meaning: To force something into a space or a schedule that is really too small for it. ---
examples: Try not to shoehorn three topics into one slide.
They shoehorned a second bedroom into the attic.
The director is shoehorning a love story into the plot.

entries.meaning: To make a person or an animal go away by waving at them. ---
examples: Don't shoo the birds off the feeder.
The waiter shooed the cat out of the kitchen.
She stood in the doorway, shooing the kids back inside.
entries.contrast: The past is shooed. Shoed belongs to shoe — putting shoes on a horse.

entries.meaning: To give someone less than they are owed, in money or in fair treatment. ---
examples: Count your change so the cashier can't shortchange you.
The clerk shortchanged him by five dollars.
Rural schools have been shortchanged for decades.

entries.meaning: To put someone or something on the short list of final candidates. ---
examples: The committee will shortlist five architects next week.
Her novel was shortlisted for the national prize.
They are shortlisting applicants all this month.
entries.русский: включать в шорт-лист, включить в окончательный список

entries.meaning: To show off in a flashy way in order to get attention. ---
examples: Good players pass the ball; they don't showboat.
He showboated after the touchdown and drew a penalty.
The crowd hates it when a driver starts showboating.
entries.русский: рисоваться, покрасоваться; выпендриваться, работать на публику

entries.meaning: To give a loud, high, sharp cry. ---
examples: The kids shriek every time the roller coaster drops.
She shrieked when the lights went out.
We could hear the brakes shrieking around the corner.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she shrieked his name), intransitive (the baby shrieked)

entries.meaning: To strip the husk or shell off corn, peas, or oysters. ---
examples: We shuck the corn outside so the husks stay off the floor.
He shucked two dozen oysters in ten minutes.
She sat on the porch shucking peas into a bowl.

entries.meaning: To move someone or something aside, usually to a less important place. ---
examples: Don't shunt the problem to another department.
The complaint was shunted from office to office.
Management keeps shunting him into jobs nobody wants.
entries.русский: отодвигать, отодвинуть в сторону; спихивать, спихнуть

entries.meaning: To tell someone to be quiet. ---
examples: Please don't shush me in front of the class.
The librarian shushed the whole table.
He kept shushing the dog while he was on the call.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel disgust or physical revulsion. ---
examples: Stories like that sicken me.
The smell of the sewer sickened everyone on the bus.
He was sickened by what he saw in the video.
entries.русский: вызывать отвращение, вызвать отвращение; внушать омерзение

entries.meaning: To avoid something by moving around it instead of dealing with it. ---
examples: Politicians sidestep questions they can't answer.
She sidestepped the puddle without breaking stride.
He has been sidestepping the issue all week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (sidestep the question), intransitive (he sidestepped quickly)
entries.contrast: The p doubles: sidestepped, sidestepping.

entries.meaning: To hit something along its side while going past it. ---
examples: One wrong turn and you sideswipe the parked cars.
A truck sideswiped her car on the interstate.
The bus was sideswiped and lost a mirror.
entries.русский: задевать боком, задеть бортом; ударять вскользь, ударить вскользь

entries.meaning: To pull someone or something away from the main subject or task. ---
examples: Let's not sidetrack the meeting with budget talk.
I sidetracked myself reading email all morning.
We got sidetracked and never finished the report.
entries.русский: отвлекать, отвлечь; сбивать с темы, сбить с темы

entries.meaning: To move sideways, quietly and a little nervously. ---
examples: Salesmen always sidle over when you look lost.
A stranger sidled up to the bar beside him.
She was sidling toward the exit before the speech ended.
entries.русский: подходить бочком, подойти бочком; двигаться боком

entries.meaning: To be a sign of something, or to make something known. ---
examples: In court, silence does not signify guilt.
A raised hand signified that she wanted the floor.
Nothing in his tone had signified anger.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie: signifies, signified.

entries.meaning: To show something as a dark outline against a lighter background. ---
examples: Backlighting will silhouette the dancer against the screen.
The sunset silhouetted two riders on the ridge.
We saw the tower silhouetted against a gray sky.
entries.русский: обрисовывать силуэтом, обрисовать силуэтом; вырисовывать на фоне
entries.contrast: The h is silent and the ending is French: sil-oo-ET.

entries.meaning: To break a religious or moral law. ---
examples: He believes we all sin in small ways every day.
She confessed that she had sinned.
The sermon was about knowingly sinning and asking forgiveness.
entries.contrast: The n doubles: sinned, sinning.

entries.meaning: To draw liquid off through a tube, or to take money away a little at a time. ---
examples: Thieves siphon gas out of parked trucks.
An official siphoned millions from the relief fund.
Money had been quietly siphoned into offshore accounts.
entries.contrast: American spelling siphon; British writing also uses syphon.

entries.meaning: To place something in a particular spot or in a particular context. ---
examples: The architects will situate the clinic near the highway.
She situated her novel in postwar Chicago.
The house is situated on a hill above the lake.

entries.meaning: To leave somewhere quickly, often to avoid trouble. ---
examples: We'd better skedaddle before the rain starts.
The kids skedaddled the moment the door opened.
They were skedaddling down the alley when the siren started.

entries.meaning: To pull a result or a picture of something out of true in one direction. ---
examples: A few huge salaries skew the average.
Bad weather skewed the turnout figures.
The sample is skewed toward younger voters.
entries.русский: искажать, исказить; смещать, сместить (в одну сторону)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (that skews the results), intransitive (the audience skews older)

entries.meaning: To push a pointed stick through food, or to attack someone sharply in words. ---
examples: Skewer the shrimp and put them on the grill.
The columnist skewered the mayor's new plan.
Chicken and peppers were skewered together.
entries.русский: насаживать на шампур, насадить; разносить в пух и прах, раскритиковать

entries.meaning: To spend less money, time, or material on something than it really needs. ---
examples: Don't skimp on the insulation.
They skimped on the foundation and paid for it later.
We have never skimped on ingredients.
entries.contrast: Takes on: ✗ skimp the budget → skimp on the budget. It always implies the shortfall was a bad idea, so it is a criticism, not a neutral word for saving money — for that, use economize or cut back. The adjective skimpy describes the result.

entries.meaning: To take the skin off something, or to scrape the skin off part of your body. ---
examples: Hunters skin the animal right away.
He fell off his bike and skinned his knee.
The rabbit had already been skinned and cleaned.
entries.русский: сдирать кожу, содрать кожу; обдирать, ободрать (колено)
entries.contrast: The n doubles: skinned, skinning.

entries.meaning: To go around the edge of something, or to avoid dealing with it directly. ---
examples: The trail skirts the lake for about a mile.
His answer skirted the real question.
We drove all evening, skirting the worst of the storm.

entries.meaning: To move or wait somewhere secretly, with bad intentions. ---
examples: Foxes skulk along the fence line after dark.
A man skulked near the loading dock for an hour.
Reporters were skulking outside the courthouse.

entries.meaning: To jump from an aircraft and fall freely before opening a parachute. ---
examples: You can skydive with an instructor on your first jump.
She skydived on her seventieth birthday.
They have been skydiving together for years.
entries.русский: прыгать с парашютом, прыгнуть с парашютом; заниматься парашютным спортом
entries.contrast: The past is regular — skydived. Skydove is heard, but it is not the standard form.

entries.meaning: To rise extremely fast. ---
examples: Rents skyrocket whenever a new campus opens.
Egg prices skyrocketed over the winter.
Demand has been skyrocketing since the video went viral.
entries.русский: резко взлетать, взлететь (о ценах); стремительно расти, вырасти

entries.meaning: To become slower or looser, or to make something slower or looser. ---
examples: Slacken the rope a little before you tie it off.
The rain slackened around noon.
Demand has slackened since the holidays.
entries.русский: ослаблять, ослабить; замедляться, замедлиться; слабеть, ослабеть
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (slacken the rope), intransitive (the pace slackened)

entries.meaning: To lean at an angle, or to present information in a biased way. ---
examples: The old floorboards slant toward the back wall.
The network slanted its coverage of the strike.
He accused the paper of slanting every headline.
entries.русский: наклонять, наклонить; иметь наклон; подавать тенденциозно, исказить подачу
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (slant the coverage), intransitive (the roof slants sharply)

entries.meaning: To spread something on thickly. ---
examples: Slather sunscreen on before you go out.
He slathered mustard across the whole sandwich.
