The walls had been slathered with cheap paint.

entries.meaning: To walk around while asleep. ---
examples: Some children sleepwalk for a few years and then stop.
He sleepwalked into the kitchen and opened the fridge.
She has been sleepwalking since the move.

entries.meaning: To insult someone by treating them as unimportant. ---
examples: He didn't mean to slight anyone with the seating chart.
Leaving her off the program slighted the whole department.
She felt slighted and stopped coming to the meetings.

entries.meaning: To let saliva run out of the mouth. ---
examples: Big dogs slobber all over the furniture.
The bulldog slobbered on my jeans.
He was slobbering into his pillow, sound asleep.

entries.meaning: To keep working or walking through something slow and exhausting. ---
examples: Most nights I just slog through email.
We slogged up the hill in the rain.
She has been slogging away at the thesis for two years.
entries.contrast: The g doubles: slogged, slogging.

entries.meaning: To lie or run at an angle rather than flat or straight. ---
examples: The yard slopes down toward the creek.
The old roof sloped so steeply we couldn't stand on it.
A long, gently sloping driveway leads to the house.
entries.русский: иметь наклон; спускаться, опускаться; наклонять, наклонить
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (slope the deck for drainage), intransitive (the lawn slopes down)

entries.meaning: To move noisily around inside a container, or to splash liquid about. ---
examples: Half-full bottles slosh the whole way home.
Coffee sloshed over the rim of the cup.
He walked slowly, the bucket sloshing against his leg.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he sloshed water on the floor), intransitive (the coffee sloshed)

entries.meaning: To fit something into a particular place or time. ---
examples: We can slot you in at four o'clock.
The producer slotted the interview after the ads.
New hires are being slotted into existing teams.
entries.русский: вставлять, вставить; помещать, поместить (в график, расписание)
entries.contrast: The t doubles: slotted, slotting.

entries.meaning: To stand, sit, or walk with the shoulders drooping forward. ---
examples: Try not to slouch while you're on camera.
He slouched in the back row the whole hour.
She was slouching over her laptop again.

entries.meaning: To shed a layer of skin or dead tissue. ---
examples: Snakes slough their skin several times a year.
The burn sloughed a layer of dead tissue.
Old cells are constantly being sloughed off.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (a snake sloughs its skin), intransitive (the dead skin sloughs away)
entries.contrast: In this sense it is said SLUF, rhyming with stuff — not like plough or through.

entries.meaning: To hit someone hard with your fist. ---
examples: Don't slug your brother over a video game.
He slugged the man who insulted his wife.
Two fans were slugging it out in the parking lot.
entries.русский: сильно бить кулаком, ударить кулаком; вмазать
entries.contrast: The g doubles: slugged, slugging.

entries.meaning: To fall sharply in value, or to drop heavily into a sitting position. ---
examples: Sales always slump in January.
He slumped into the chair without a word.
Attendance has been slumping for three seasons.
entries.русский: резко падать, упасть (о ценах, спросе); опускаться, ссутулиться

entries.meaning: To run words together so that they are hard to understand. ---
examples: Painkillers can make you slur your words.
He slurred the last half of the sentence.
She was slurring badly by the end of the night.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he slurred his words), intransitive (she was slurring badly)
entries.contrast: The r doubles: slurred, slurring.

entries.meaning: To turn the corners of your mouth up to show that you are pleased or friendly. ---
examples: Try to smile for the photo.
She smiled when she saw the address on the envelope.
He was smiling the whole way home.
entries.contrast: You smile at someone: she smiled at me, never she smiled me.

entries.meaning: To smile in a smug or knowing way that annoys other people. ---
examples: Don't smirk when someone else gets it wrong.
He smirked at the question and said nothing.
She kept smirking through the entire apology.

entries.meaning: To follow a long, winding path, or to push a flexible tool through a pipe. ---
examples: The road snakes through the canyon for twenty miles.
A line of cars snaked around the block.
The plumber is snaking the kitchen drain right now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (snake the drain), intransitive (the river snakes north)

entries.meaning: To catch an animal in a trap, or to catch a person out. ---
examples: Poachers snare rabbits along the fence line.
The sting operation snared three officials.
He was snared by his own emails.
entries.русский: ловить в силки, поймать; заманивать в ловушку, заманить

entries.meaning: To growl with the teeth showing, or to speak in an angry, hostile way. ---
examples: Stray dogs snarl when you get too close.
He snarled an answer and hung up.
The guard stood there, snarling at anyone who came near.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he snarled a warning), intransitive (the dog snarled)

entries.meaning: To laugh quietly and unkindly. ---
examples: Students snicker whenever he mispronounces a name.
Someone snickered in the back of the room.
They were still snickering about it at lunch.
entries.contrast: American English uses snicker; British writing uses snigger.

entries.meaning: To breathe in noisily through a blocked or running nose. ---
examples: The kids sniffle all through allergy season.
She sniffled her way through the whole movie.
He sat sniffling into a paper towel.

entries.meaning: To cut something with quick, small strokes of scissors. ---
examples: Snip the tag off before you wear it.
The nurse snipped the bandage in two.
He stood there snipping at the hedge.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (snip the thread), intransitive (she snipped at the loose ends)
entries.contrast: The p doubles: snipped, snipping.

entries.meaning: To force air noisily out through the nose, often in scorn or laughter. ---
examples: Horses snort when they are nervous.
He snorted at the suggestion and walked off.
She was snorting with laughter by the second verse.

entries.meaning: To grow bigger and faster in a way that is hard to stop. ---
examples: Small repairs snowball into a full renovation.
The complaint snowballed into a federal investigation.
Costs have been snowballing since the delay.
entries.русский: расти как снежный ком, нарастать, нарасти; разрастаться, разрастись

entries.meaning: To treat a room so that sound cannot get in or out. ---
examples: We need to soundproof the practice room.
They soundproofed the basement before the baby came.
The studio has been fully soundproofed.

entries.meaning: To go bad, or to turn a relationship or a mood unpleasant. ---
examples: Milk will sour in a day at that temperature.
The deal soured after the audit.
Months of delays have been souring public opinion.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the scandal soured relations), intransitive (the milk soured)

entries.meaning: To find and obtain materials, parts, or staff from a supplier. ---
examples: We source the beans directly from growers.
They sourced the steel from three different mills.
All the wood is sourced locally.
entries.русский: закупать, закупить; находить поставщика; добывать, добыть

entries.meaning: To arrange things with gaps between them, in a line or over time. ---
examples: Space the seedlings about a foot apart.
The doctor spaced the injections three weeks apart.
The fence posts are evenly spaced.
entries.русский: располагать с промежутками, расположить; распределять, распределить (по времени)

entries.meaning: To stretch across something, in distance or in time. ---
examples: Two bridges span the river downtown.
Her career spanned four decades.
The study, spanning twelve countries, took six years.
entries.contrast: The n doubles: spanned, spanning.

entries.meaning: To hit a child on the bottom with an open hand as punishment. ---
examples: Most schools no longer spank students.
His father spanked him for lying.
She grew up without ever being spanked.

entries.meaning: To remove the ovaries of a female animal so that it cannot breed. ---
examples: The shelter will spay every cat before adoption.
We spayed her at six months.
All our dogs are spayed or neutered.
entries.contrast: Spay is for females; a male animal is neutered.

entries.meaning: To join two pieces end to end so that they work as one. ---
examples: You can splice the two cables with a connector.
The editor spliced the two takes together.
A gene had been spliced into the plant's DNA.

entries.meaning: To imitate something in a joking way, or to fake an identity electronically. ---
examples: Late-night shows spoof the debates every four years.
Scammers spoofed the bank's phone number.
The ad is spoofing a famous movie trailer.

entries.meaning: To frighten a person or an animal suddenly. ---
examples: Loud noises spook the horses.
The news spooked investors.
Something must have spooked her, because she left early.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the noise spooked the herd), intransitive (the horse spooked and bolted)

entries.meaning: To move food from one place to another with a spoon. ---
examples: Spoon the sauce over the fish before serving.
He spooned soup into a thermos.
She was spooning yogurt straight from the container.
entries.русский: черпать ложкой, зачерпнуть; накладывать ложкой, наложить

entries.meaning: To sit or lie with your arms and legs spread out, or to spread over a large area in an untidy way. ---
examples: Teenagers sprawl across the couch the moment they get home.
He sprawled in the armchair and fell asleep.
The city has sprawled far out into the desert.

entries.meaning: To spray something with a fine mist of liquid. ---
examples: I spritz the herbs with water every morning.
She spritzed perfume on her wrists before leaving.
The stylist was spritzing my hair while we talked.
entries.contrast: Verbs ending in -tz add -es in the third person: she spritzes.

entries.meaning: To reject someone or something proudly or scornfully. ---
examples: Voters spurn candidates who talk down to them.
She spurned his apology and walked out.
Having spurned two offers, he suddenly had none.
entries.русский: отвергать, отвергнуть; пренебрегать, отказываться с презрением

entries.meaning: To come out in a sudden strong stream, or to move with a sudden burst of speed. ---
examples: Water spurts from that crack whenever the pump starts.
Steam spurted out of the broken valve.
He was spurting ahead of the pack on the final lap.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the wound spurted blood), intransitive (water spurted from the pipe)

entries.meaning: To make a series of soft popping sounds, or to speak in a broken, flustered way. ---
examples: Old engines sputter in cold weather.
The candle sputtered twice and went out.
He stood there sputtering, unable to finish the sentence.
entries.русский: фыркать, чихать (о моторе); лепетать, бормотать от возмущения
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he sputtered an excuse), intransitive (the engine sputtered)

entries.meaning: To make two things agree with each other, or to multiply a number by itself. ---
examples: His account does not square with the security footage.
She squared her shoulders and knocked on the door.
Four squared is sixteen.
entries.русский: согласовываться, совпадать; приводить в соответствие; возводить в квадрат
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (square the numbers), intransitive (his story doesn't square with hers)
entries.contrast: In the sense of agreeing it takes with: that squares with what I heard.

entries.meaning: To make a loud harsh cry, or to complain loudly. ---
examples: Gulls squawk over the parking lot all summer.
The parrot squawked when the cat walked in.
Season-ticket holders are squawking about the price hike.
entries.русский: пронзительно кричать (о птице); громко возмущаться, вопить
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the radio squawked a warning), intransitive (the parrot squawked)

entries.meaning: To make a long, high-pitched cry or sound. ---
examples: Kids squeal when the roller coaster drops.
The tires squealed as he took the corner.
She was squealing with delight over the puppy.

entries.meaning: To put a quick and complete stop to something such as a rumor or a protest. ---
examples: The mayor moved fast to squelch the rumor.
Management squelched every attempt to organize.
Our boots were squelching across the wet field.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (squelch the rumor), intransitive (our boots squelched in the mud)

entries.meaning: To twist your body because you are uncomfortable or embarrassed. ---
examples: Small children squirm through long ceremonies.
He squirmed when the reporter asked about the money.
She sat squirming in the dentist's chair.

entries.meaning: To crush something soft, or to make a wet sucking sound under pressure. ---
examples: Try not to squish the bread at the bottom of the bag.
He squished the spider with a napkin.
Wet leaves were squishing under our shoes.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (squish a bug), intransitive (mud squished underfoot)

entries.meaning: To speak with pauses and repeated sounds, usually out of nervousness. ---
examples: He tends to stammer when he is put on the spot.
She stammered out an apology and sat down.
The boy answered, stammering over every other word.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (stammer an apology), intransitive (he stammers when he is nervous)
entries.contrast: Stutter is the everyday synonym; stammer sounds a little more formal.

entries.meaning: To stop something from flowing out, especially blood or money. ---
examples: Medics use direct pressure to stanch heavy bleeding.
A folded towel stanched the wound until help arrived.
The airline is still trying to stanch its losses.
entries.contrast: Staunch with a u is the adjective — a staunch supporter. American English spells the verb stanch.

entries.meaning: To look at someone or something for a long time without moving your eyes. ---
examples: It is rude to stare at strangers.
He stared at the screen for a full minute without blinking.
She caught me staring and smiled.
entries.contrast: Stare takes at: stare at the painting, never stare the painting.

entries.meaning: To send someone to a particular place to work or stand guard. ---
examples: The army will station two brigades near the border.
They stationed a guard at every entrance.
Her father was stationed in Germany for three years.

entries.meaning: To force something through, or defeat someone, by sheer weight and without listening. ---
examples: A big majority can steamroll any amendment it dislikes.
The bill was steamrolled through in a single night.
He kept steamrolling everyone who tried to speak.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (steamroll the opposition), intransitive (the bill steamrolled through the senate)

entries.meaning: To prepare yourself mentally for something difficult or painful. ---
examples: Nurses learn to steel themselves against bad news.
He steeled himself and opened the letter.
She had steeled herself for a much worse verdict.
entries.русский: собираться с духом, собраться с духом; закалять, ожесточать
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like steal. In this sense the object is reflexive: steel yourself.

entries.meaning: To become steeper, or to make something steeper. ---
examples: The trail steepens sharply after the bridge.
The decline steepened in the last hour of trading.
The climb has steepened with every mile.
entries.русский: становиться круче; делать круче, увеличивать крутизну
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (steepen the ramp), intransitive (the trail steepens)

entries.meaning: To judge people by a fixed, oversimplified idea of the group they belong to. ---
examples: Ads often stereotype older customers as helpless.
The movie stereotyped every character from the South.
Teenagers hate being stereotyped as lazy.
entries.русский: воспринимать шаблонно; навешивать ярлыки, судить по стереотипу

entries.meaning: To become hard or tense, or to make something firmer or stricter. ---
examples: Cold air makes the joints stiffen.
She stiffened when he said her name.
Congress has stiffened the penalties for fraud.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (stiffen the rules), intransitive (he stiffened at the sound)

entries.meaning: To treat something or someone as shameful and unacceptable. ---
examples: We should not stigmatize people who ask for help.
Poverty stigmatized whole neighborhoods for decades.
Mental illness is still stigmatized in many workplaces.
entries.contrast: British English writes stigmatise; American English uses -ize.

entries.meaning: To state something clearly as a condition of an agreement. ---
examples: Most leases stipulate that pets are not allowed.
The will stipulated that the house be sold.
Payment terms are stipulated in section four.

entries.meaning: To build up a large supply of something for future use. ---
examples: Hospitals stockpile masks before flu season.
Shoppers stockpiled rice and canned food.
The country has been stockpiling fuel all winter.

entries.meaning: To make a fire burn harder, or to make a feeling or situation more intense. ---
examples: Cheap credit can stoke inflation.
His remarks stoked the anger of the crowd.
Rumors of a shortage are stoking panic buying.

entries.meaning: To be able to accept or endure something unpleasant. ---
examples: I can't stomach another meeting like that one.
She stomached the insult without saying a word.
He has never been able to stomach horror movies.
entries.contrast: The final -ch is pronounced /k/: STUM-uhk. The verb is almost always negative: can't stomach.

entries.meaning: To block progress by refusing to answer questions or cooperate. ---
examples: Companies often stonewall when regulators call.
The agency stonewalled reporters for months.
They are stonewalling the investigation with paperwork.
entries.русский: чинить препятствия; уклоняться от ответов, тянуть время
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (stonewall the investigation), intransitive (the witness stonewalled)

entries.meaning: To bend the upper body forward and down, or to lower yourself morally. ---
examples: You have to stoop to get through that doorway.
He stooped to pick up the coins.
She would never stoop to lying about a colleague.
entries.contrast: Stoop to + noun or -ing means sink to that level: stoop to name-calling.

entries.meaning: To sit or stand with a leg on each side of something, or to lie across two sides of a line or an issue. ---
examples: The town straddles the state line.
She straddled the bike and pushed off.
He has been straddling both sides of the debate for months.
entries.русский: сидеть верхом (расставив ноги); стоять по обе стороны; занимать двойственную позицию

entries.meaning: To attack a target on the ground with gunfire from a low-flying aircraft. ---
examples: Warplanes strafe the road whenever the convoy moves in daylight.
The jets strafed a column of trucks outside the city.
The village had been strafed twice before the ceasefire.
entries.русский: обстреливать с бреющего полёта, обстрелять с воздуха

entries.meaning: To plan carefully how to achieve a goal. ---
examples: The team meets every Monday to strategize.
They strategized for hours before the negotiation.
We spent the whole weekend strategizing about the launch.
entries.contrast: British English writes strategise; American English uses -ize.

entries.meaning: To arrange or divide something into separate layers or levels. ---
examples: Researchers stratify the sample by age and income.
A century of easy money stratified the city into two worlds.
The lake has stratified into a warm layer and a cold one.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (stratify the sample by age), intransitive (the lake stratifies in summer)
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie-: stratifies, stratified.

entries.meaning: To mark something with long thin lines, or to move very fast in a straight line. ---
examples: Rain streaks those windows every night.
A meteor streaked across the sky just after midnight.
Her dark hair is streaked with gray.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rain streaked the windows), intransitive (a meteor streaked across the sky)

entries.meaning: To arrange the parts of something into an organized system. ---
examples: Let's structure the report around three questions.
She structured the deal so that no one paid tax up front.
The course is structured as six short modules.

entries.meaning: To hit your toe painfully against something. ---
examples: I stub my toe on that step almost every morning.
He stubbed his toe on the coffee table in the dark.
She was limping after stubbing her toe on the curb.
entries.contrast: A single vowel plus a single consonant doubles it: stub → stubbed, stubbing.

entries.meaning: To cover a surface with many small objects scattered across it. ---
examples: Tiny lights stud the ceiling of the old theater.
The baker studded the loaf with olives.
The sky was studded with stars.
entries.contrast: The consonant doubles: stud → studded, studding.

entries.meaning: To shock or bore someone so much that they cannot think clearly. ---
examples: Long legal documents stupefy most readers.
The verdict stupefied everyone in the courtroom.
He sat stupefied by the noise and the lights.
entries.русский: ошеломлять, ошеломить; изумлять, приводить в оцепенение
entries.contrast: Note the spelling: stupefy, not stupify, even though the adjective is stupid.

entries.meaning: To present something in a simplified, artificial style instead of realistically. ---
examples: Japanese prints stylize waves into curling lines.
The director stylized every fight scene.
The logo is a heavily stylized letter M.

entries.meaning: To block someone or something from making progress. ---
examples: Budget rules stymie almost every new program.
Bad weather stymied the search for two days.
The bill has been stymied in committee since spring.
entries.русский: ставить в тупик; мешать, помешать; блокировать
entries.contrast: The -ing form keeps the e: stymieing (the spelling stymying is also seen).

entries.meaning: To pay another company to do part of the work you have agreed to do. ---
examples: Big builders subcontract almost everything but the frame.
They subcontracted the wiring to a local firm.
Half the job had been subcontracted before we found out.
entries.русский: передавать на субподряд, отдать в субподряд
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (subcontract the wiring), intransitive (they subcontract to local firms)
entries.contrast: The noun is stressed at the front, SUB-kahn-trakt; the verb at the end, sub-kuhn-TRAKT.

entries.meaning: To divide something that is already a part into still smaller parts. ---
examples: Planners want to subdivide the old farm into forty lots.
He subdivided the chapter into three sections.
The property was subdivided back in the 1970s.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (subdivide the land), intransitive (the cells subdivide)

entries.meaning: To make someone or something undergo something unpleasant. ---
examples: Border agents may subject any traveler to a search.
The company subjected every batch to a stress test.
Prisoners were subjected to weeks of interrogation.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, suhb-JEKT; the noun on the first, SUB-jikt. It takes to.

entries.meaning: To bring a people or a place under your control by force. ---
examples: No army can subjugate a population forever.
Rome subjugated the entire region within a decade.
The islands remained subjugated for two centuries.

entries.meaning: To rent out to someone else a place that you are renting yourself. ---
examples: Many students sublease their apartments for the summer.
She subleased the studio to a friend in June.
The office has been subleased twice since we moved out.
entries.русский: сдавать в субаренду, пересдавать; снимать в субаренду
entries.contrast: Sublet means the same thing but is irregular: sublet → sublet → sublet.

entries.meaning: To redirect a strong impulse into an activity that other people accept. ---
examples: Athletes often sublimate anger into training.
He sublimated his grief into a long, strange novel.
That energy has to go somewhere, and most of us end up sublimating it.

entries.meaning: To treat one thing as less important than another. ---
examples: Good editors subordinate style to clarity.
He subordinated his own career to hers for a decade.
Everything was subordinated to the deadline.
entries.русский: подчинять, подчинить; ставить на второе место
entries.contrast: The verb ends in -nayt; the noun and adjective end in -nuht: my subordinate (suh-BOR-duh-nuht).

entries.meaning: To pay regularly to receive something, or to agree with an idea. ---
examples: Millions subscribe to the streaming service.
I subscribed to that paper for almost ten years.
She has never subscribed to the theory that talent is fixed.
entries.contrast: Subscribe takes to: subscribe to a magazine, subscribe to a view.

entries.meaning: To stay alive on a very small amount of food or money. ---
examples: Whole villages subsist on what they can grow.
The crew subsisted on rice and dried fish for a month.
They have been subsisting on savings since the layoff.
entries.contrast: Takes on: subsist on bread and water.

entries.meaning: To provide evidence that proves a claim is true. ---
examples: Reporters have to substantiate every accusation they print.
Nothing in the file substantiated his story.
The claims were never substantiated.

entries.meaning: To include something within a larger group or category. ---
examples: The new agency will subsume three older offices.
The company subsumed its rival's staff without a single layoff.
Local dialects were gradually subsumed into the standard language.
entries.русский: включать в состав, поглощать, поглотить; относить к категории

entries.meaning: To secretly weaken or undermine a system, a rule, or an authority. ---
examples: Cheap fakes subvert trust in every photograph.
The leaks subverted the whole negotiation.
He was accused of subverting the election.

entries.meaning: To stop resisting something, or to die from an illness or injury. ---
examples: Most dieters succumb to temptation by February.
He succumbed to his injuries two days later.
She has finally succumbed to the pressure and resigned.
entries.русский: поддаваться, поддаться; не устоять; скончаться (от болезни)
entries.contrast: The final b is silent, and the verb takes to: succumb to pressure.

entries.meaning: To feed a baby or a young animal with milk from the breast, or to take milk that way. ---
examples: Ewes suckle their lambs for about three months.
The kittens suckled until they fell asleep.
The calf was still suckling at six weeks.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the ewe suckles her lambs), intransitive (the lamb suckled for an hour)

entries.meaning: To feel pain or distress, or to experience something bad. ---
examples: Nobody should suffer in silence.
The company suffered heavy losses last quarter.
She has suffered from migraines since childhood.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (suffer heavy losses), intransitive (he suffered in silence)
entries.contrast: For illnesses use from: suffer from asthma, not suffer asthma.

entries.meaning: To be enough for a particular purpose. ---
examples: A one-page summary will suffice.
One example sufficed to end the argument.
Nothing he said suffices as an explanation.
entries.contrast: The fixed phrase suffice it to say introduces a short version of a long story.

entries.meaning: To spread through or over something, filling it with color, light, or feeling. ---
examples: Late sun suffuses the room with orange light.
A blush suffused her cheeks.
The whole book is suffused with nostalgia.

entries.meaning: To make bad news sound better than it really is. ---
examples: I won't sugarcoat it: we are two months behind.
The memo sugarcoated what everyone already knew.
She gave me the numbers straight, without sugarcoating anything.

entries.meaning: To damage someone's good name or spoil something that was clean or pure. ---
examples: One bad hire can sully a whole team's reputation.
The scandal sullied a career built over thirty years.
He refused to have his name sullied by that deal.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie-: sullies, sullied.

entries.meaning: To sit or lie in the sun in order to get a tan. ---
examples: Tourists sunbathe on those rocks all afternoon.
We sunbathed on the roof until the wind picked up.
She was sunbathing when the storm rolled in.
entries.contrast: The ending is voiced, like bathe /beɪð/, not like the noun bath.

entries.meaning: To make something far more powerful or effective than before. ---
examples: Cheap money can supercharge a housing market.
The grant supercharged their research.
Sales have been supercharged by a single video.
entries.русский: резко усиливать, форсировать; придавать мощный импульс

entries.meaning: To place one image or idea on top of another so that both can be seen. ---
examples: The app lets you superimpose text on a photo.
They superimposed the old map on the new one.
A date was superimposed in the corner of every frame.

entries.meaning: To take the place of something older or less effective. ---
examples: The new rules supersede the ones printed in the handbook.
Email largely superseded the office memo.
This contract has been superseded by the 2024 version.
entries.русский: заменять, заменить; приходить на смену, вытеснять
entries.contrast: Spelled -sede, not -cede: compare precede, concede, recede.

entries.meaning: To take the place of someone or something, often by force or by scheming. ---
examples: Streaming did not entirely supplant the movie theater.
A younger rival supplanted him as party leader.
Coal has largely been supplanted by gas.

entries.meaning: To charge someone an extra amount on top of the normal price. ---
examples: Some airlines surcharge for every checked bag.
The hotel surcharged us for a late checkout.
Card payments are surcharged at two percent.

entries.meaning: To come up to the surface, or to become known. ---
examples: Old photos surface every time someone runs for office.
New details surfaced a week after the crash.
The submarine had surfaced two miles offshore.
entries.русский: всплывать, всплыть; появляться, выявляться; выносить на поверхность
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (surface the problem at the meeting), intransitive (new details surfaced)

entries.meaning: To guess something from the little evidence you have. ---
examples: Readers will surmise the ending long before it arrives.
She surmised from his tone that the news was bad.
Surmising that no one was home, he left the package on the step.

entries.meaning: To deal successfully with a serious difficulty. ---
examples: Few startups surmount the first two years.
She surmounted every obstacle the system put in her way.
Having surmounted the language barrier, he found the job easy.

entries.meaning: To watch a person or a place closely, especially as police or security. ---
examples: Agents surveil the building around the clock.
Police surveilled the house for three weeks.
Employees who are constantly surveilled do not work any better.
entries.русский: вести наблюдение (за), следить; держать под наблюдением
entries.contrast: The noun is surveillance, but the verb is just surveil, with a doubled l in surveilled, surveilling.

entries.meaning: To close a wound with stitches. ---
examples: Residents learn to suture on pig skin.
The surgeon sutured the incision in four minutes.
The cut had already been sutured by the time I got there.

entries.meaning: To wipe something, or take a sample from it, with a small piece of absorbent material. ---
examples: Nurses swab your arm before the shot.
They swabbed his cheek for DNA.
Everyone was swabbed at the door before the flight.
entries.contrast: The consonant doubles: swab → swabbed, swabbing.

entries.meaning: To walk or behave in a confident, boastful way. ---
examples: Some players swagger onto the court before they have won anything.
He swaggered into the room ten minutes late.
She came swaggering down the hall with the trophy.
entries.русский: расхаживать с важным видом, важничать; хорохориться

entries.meaning: To hit something, especially an insect, with a quick flat blow. ---
examples: I swat mosquitoes all evening on that porch.
She swatted the fly with a rolled-up magazine.
He kept swatting at the wasp instead of walking away.
entries.contrast: The consonant doubles: swat → swatted, swatting.

entries.meaning: To drink something in large mouthfuls, usually straight from the container. ---
examples: Runners swig water at every station.
He swigged the last of the coffee and stood up.
She was swigging iced tea straight from the jug.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (swig a soda), intransitive (he swigged from the bottle)
entries.contrast: The consonant doubles: swig → swigged, swigging.

entries.meaning: To cheat someone out of money by deceiving them. ---
examples: Fake charities swindle thousands of donors every year.
He swindled his own clients for nearly a decade.
Retirees were swindled out of their savings.

entries.meaning: To turn around a fixed central point. ---
examples: These stools swivel all the way around.
She swiveled in her chair to face me.
He sat swiveling back and forth the whole time he talked.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (swivel the chair), intransitive (she swiveled around)
entries.contrast: American English keeps one l: swiveled, swiveling; British English doubles it.

entries.meaning: To be overwhelmed with delight or admiration, or, in older usage, to faint. ---
examples: Critics swoon over anything she writes.
Fans swooned when he walked onstage.
The audience was still swooning an hour after the encore.
entries.русский: млеть, таять (от восторга); падать в обморок
entries.contrast: In the modern sense it takes over: swoon over a singer.

entries.meaning: To make two or more things happen or move at exactly the same time. ---
examples: Let's synchronize our watches before we split up.
The dancers synchronized their steps perfectly.
The app is synchronizing your photos with the cloud.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (synchronize the files), intransitive (the two clocks synchronize)
entries.contrast: American English spells it synchronize; the -ise form (synchronise) is British.

entries.meaning: To sell a column, cartoon, or television show to many newspapers or stations at once. ---
examples: The network plans to syndicate the show next fall.
They syndicated the comic strip nationwide in 1994.
Her column is syndicated in more than two hundred papers.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in a full vowel — SIN-duh-kayt — but the noun a syndicate ends in a schwa: SIN-duh-kuht.

entries.meaning: To organize something into an orderly, consistent system.
examples: The new director wants to systematize hiring.
They systematized the filing system last spring.
Once the records had been systematized, a search took seconds.
